text: The Pittsburgh Professional Hockey Club, also known as the Pittsburgh Professionals or Pittsburgh Pros, was a professional ice hockey team that competed in the International Professional Hockey League (IPHL) from 1904 to 1907. The team played its home games at Duquesne Garden, which had a capacity of 5,000 seats, and was the first inter-city professional hockey team based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The Pros' roster included several early professional hockey stars, most notably Hod Stuart, who was regarded in certain hockey circles as the "greatest hockey player in the world." The club was formed from players of the Western Pennsylvania Hockey League (WPHL), which disbanded after the 1904 season. During the 1902–03 WPHL season, the Pittsburgh Bankers faced the Portage Lakes Hockey Club of Houghton, Michigan, in a four-game series for the "Pro Championship of the United States," which Portage Lakes won 2–1 with one game tied, despite being outscored 11–6. In the fall of 1903, James R. Dee of Houghton began discussions with WPHL representatives to establish a national hockey association. The following season, Portage Lakes played professional exhibition games and raided Pittsburgh teams for top players like Riley Hern and Bruce Stuart. After the 1903–04 WPHL season, the Pittsburgh Victorias lost to Portage Lakes in the "American Championship" battle. On November 5, 1904, a meeting was held involving prominent business leaders from Pittsburgh, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, and Northern Michigan, where teams from Houghton (Portage Lakes), Pittsburgh (Pros), Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario (Canadian Soo), Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan (Michigan Soo Indians), and Calumet & Laurium, Michigan (Calumet Miners) were accepted into the new league. At this meeting, the Canadian Soo proposed a revenue-sharing plan dividing gate receipts 60–40 in favor of the home team, which made the long travel to Pittsburgh feasible. Although Pittsburgh was larger in population than other IPHL markets, its fan base was largely working-class, and local supporters nicknamed the team the "Coal Heavers." The Pros struggled in their first season, finishing with an 8–15–1 record and placing fourth. The team was also affected by the death of player William "Peg" Duval on June 7, 1905, due to alcoholism; Duval had been suspended in December 1904 without pay for being unfit to play, returned to score the winning goal against Calumet on January 7, 1905, and was permanently released in February 1905 for failing to maintain fitness. A Pittsburgh Press report stated that "Peggy" could perform at a high level when fit, but alcohol "seemed to have a fascination for him," leading to his downfall. In the 1905–06 season, the team acquired Hod Stuart, who was suspended before the season began by western teams for winning too many championships and being too rough, but was reinstated on December 30 and joined the Pros. The Pros finished third in the standings that season, competing with Portage Lakes and the Michigan Soo Indians for first place. Stuart later left the team after a dispute, but the roster still included notable players such as Tommy Smith and Horace Gaul from the Ottawa Hockey Club and Jimmy Gardner from the Montreal Wanderers, along with alumni Jack Winchester and Lorne Campbell. Campbell and Smith finished ahead of future Hall of Famers Didier Pitre, Newsy Lalonde, and Bruce Stuart in scoring, but the team again finished third. The team's uniform colors varied over time, including gold (or yellow or orange) and black, maroon and white, and blue and white. The IPHL and the Pittsburgh Professionals operated until after the 1906–07 season, but the revenue-sharing plan—granting visiting teams 40% of gate receipts—proved unsustainable, leading to insufficient funds to cover player salaries and ultimately the collapse of both the team and the league. The league's failure resulted in the revival of the WPHL as a fully professional league. Several members of the Pittsburgh Professionals later became inductees to the Hockey Hall of Fame.
